key_insight: Reported gains from randomly perturbing language-model weights may not require discovering nearby task-specific experts. Keeping the model frozen and adding random biases to its output logits can match or exceed full-weight perturbations, according to the provided abstract excerpt.
problem_solved: Tests whether improvements attributed to the Neural Thickets hypothesis truly depend on dense neighborhoods of experts in weight space—or can arise from simpler changes to model outputs.
method: Reproduce the reported gains from random Gaussian perturbations of pretrained model weights.
Restrict perturbations to a single decoder block and test how much improvement remains.
Keep all model weights frozen, add random output-logit biases, and compare against full-weight perturbations.
impact: Practitioners should test simple output-level baselines before attributing performance gains to weight-space geometry. These findings challenge the necessity of weight perturbations, without establishing that nearby task-specific experts do not exist.
visual_elements: Three-path diagram comparing full-weight perturbations, single-block perturbations, and frozen-model logit biases.
Conceptual weight-space neighborhood contrasted with a direct output-bias adjustment.
Qualitative comparison highlighting substantial gains from one-block perturbations and competitive frozen-model results, without inventing numerical scores.
Frozen-model icon feeding into a logit vector with added random offsets.
paper_title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
paper_authors: Nicolas Dufour, Elouan Gardès, Amil Dravid, Patrick Pérez, Loic Landrieu
